newsitem.title: CONGO: Congo factions fight for airport.
newsitem.headline: Congo factions fight for airport.

text.p: Congolese President Pascal Lissouba's troops fought to hold on to Brazzaville airport against an enemy assault as an already sick truce died.
Artillery fire boomed for hours on Wednesday across a capital divided between forces loyal to Lissouba and the militia of his rival Denis Sassou Nguesso. A neutral leader controls a third part.
"Hundreds, maybe thousands of people are fleeing north and south to the edges of the city," said a Red Cross spokesman in the twin capital of Kinshasa, just over the Congo river in the former Zaire.
Panicky government troops assaulted French ambassador Raymond Cesaire, beat up his bodyguard and shot at escorts as they left Lissouba's palace after a meeting, witnesses said.
Diplomats said Sassou, for 13 years Congo's one-party president until Lissouba defeated him in free elections in 1992, had advanced towards the strategically vital airport.
"It seems Sassou has taken at least part of the airport and created a new military situation which is making the government troops nervous," one said.
Shells slammed into the landmark high-rise Sofitel hotel beside the Congo river and landed around the nearby French embassy, just 200 metres (yards) from the frontline.
Some 30 French nationals, mostly diplomats and gendarmes, took refuge in the embassy compound.
The area calmed as night fell but gunfire could still be heard nearer to the airport.
A pilot who was to have flown into Brazzaville said he was warned away by air traffic officials who said Sassou's "Cobra" militia had taken the nearby Aeroclub.
The Aeroclub was base for 1,250 French troops who pulled out last week after evacuating thousands of foreign nationals.
France, its influence waning in ex-Zaire and its troops under fire in the neighbouring Central African Republic, showed little sign of venturing back militarily into the former French Congo.
President Jacques Chirac said he would not provide troops for a U.N.-backed peacekeeping force for Brazzaville.
So far only Togo and Senegal have pledged to contribute to the mission, but a stable ceasefire is a U.N. precondition for its dispatch.
"France would not join in the force itself but would certainly provide it with support and technical aid," Chirac said.
Brazzaville's first 12 days of fighting, until the truce began a week ago, claimed an estimated 1,000 lives.
Many corpses still lie rotting where they died on the boulevards of the former French colonial capital, too dangerous for the Red Cross to reach even during the partial ceasefire.
The battle for control of Brazzaville has so far left the rest of the oil-producing country unscathed.
Political mediation efforts are aimed at putting back on track presidential elections due on July 27 but postponed due to the fighting. Little progress has been made.
